summary: Specifies the original Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, a lighter way to reach an X.500 Directory without the heavy resource needs of the full Directory Access Protocol. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1777, RFC 3494.

plainLanguage.summary: A big library has a complicated desk process for finding a book. This memo describes a quick, simple window where you can ask the librarian the same questions.

questions: what operations does ldap version 2 support
how does ldap differ from x500 dap
subtitle: A lightweight way for simple clients to read and update an X.500 Directory over TCP.

tldr.problem: The X.500 Directory Access Protocol (DAP) needs heavy session and presentation machinery, which makes it costly for simple management and browser applications to use the Directory.
tldr.mechanism: LDAP carries a small set of operations (bind, search, modify, add, delete, modify RDN, compare, abandon, unbind) directly over TCP, uses plain strings for names, and a restricted BER encoding.
tldr.outcome: This RFC describes version 2 of LDAP. It is now Historic and was replaced by RFC 1777 and RFC 3494.

today: RFC 1487 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1777 and RFC 3494, so it should be read only as the original LDAP version 2 specification.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight Protocol
sections.content:
Interest in X.500 Directory technology on the Internet had led to efforts to cut its high cost of entry, such as the Directory Assistance Service and DIXIE. Those efforts were tied to particular implementations, so their reach was limited. This document tries to define a Directory protocol alternative without depending on any particular implementation.

The abstract names the target: simple management applications and browser applications that need simple read and write access to the Directory. LDAP is meant as a complement to the DAP, not a replacement for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The full Directory protocol is like a huge rulebook. This one is a short cheat sheet for programs that only need to look things up or make small changes.

sections.title: Protocol Model and Transport
sections.content:
The model is clients performing operations against servers. A client sends a request, the server does the necessary work on the Directory, and the server returns a response with results or errors. One goal is to keep clients simple so that many applications can use the Directory.

Requests and responses do not have to be synchronous: several operations can be outstanding, and responses may come in any order, as long as every request that needs a response eventually gets one. Servers are expected to handle referrals themselves. The protocol has no way to hand a referral back to the client. The protocol maps onto a strict subset of the Directory abstract service, so the DAP can provide it cleanly.

LDAP needs a connection-oriented, reliable transport where all 8 bits of each octet are significant. Two mappings are defined. Over TCP, each message goes straight onto the byte stream and servers should listen on port 389. Over the Connection Oriented Transport Service, each message maps onto one T-Data.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the server a question and it does all the hard running around for you. You only get the final answer, and you can ask several questions before the first answer comes back.

sections.title: The LDAPMessage Envelope and Results
sections.content:
Every operation travels inside a common envelope, the LDAPMessage. It holds a messageID and the operation itself. The message ID must differ from any other request outstanding in the session, and it is echoed in every response to that request.

Names are plain strings. A Distinguished Name is carried as an LDAPDN using the string form from RFC 1485. Attribute types are the textual names used in the Directory standards, for example organizationName. If an implementation cannot map a type to a name, it may use the dotted object identifier as a string, such as 2.5.4.10.

Most responses carry an LDAPResult with a resultCode, a matchedDN and an optional human-readable errorMessage. Codes include success (0), noSuchObject (32), invalidCredentials (49) and other (80). The error message is not standardized, so implementations should not rely on its text.
sections.plainLanguage: Every question goes in an envelope with a number on it. The answer comes back in an envelope with the same number, so you know which question it belongs to.

sections.title: The Operations
sections.content:
A session begins with a Bind, which must be the first request. It carries a version number (this document describes version 2, and there is no version negotiation), a name, and credentials. The choices are simple (a cleartext password, also used for anonymous binds with an empty value), or Kerberos version 4 tickets for either the LDAP server or the DSA. Unbind ends the session and has no response.

Search takes a base object, a scope (baseObject, singleLevel or wholeSubtree), an alias-dereferencing mode, a size limit, a time limit in seconds, a filter and the attributes wanted. A value of 0 for either limit means no limit. Filters combine and, or and not with equality, substring, greater-or-equal, less-or-equal, present and approximate matches. The server returns zero or more entries followed by a single result. An X.500 list can be emulated by a one-level search and a read by a base-object search.

Modify applies a list of add, delete and replace changes in order as a single atomic operation, so an error means nothing was changed. Add creates an entry (every name component except the last must already exist), and Delete removes a leaf entry only. Modify RDN changes the last component of an entry's name. Compare tests an assertion against an entry. Abandon asks the server to drop an outstanding operation by message ID and has no response.
sections.plainLanguage: You can knock on the door (bind), ask for things, add or change things, and say goodbye (unbind). If you change your mind about a question, you can say never mind.

sections.title: Encoding on the Wire
sections.content:
Protocol elements are written in ASN.1 and encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER). Because parts of BER are costly, LDAP adds two restrictions: only the definite form of length encoding is used, and bit strings and octet strings are encoded in the primitive form only.

Appendix A of the RFC gives the complete ASN.1 definition.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are packed into a standard box format, but LDAP picks only the simple ways of packing so the boxes are easy to open.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: This version offers only simple authentication with a cleartext password and Kerberos version 4 authentication. The RFC expects future versions of LDAP to support other authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The only locks on the door are a plain password anyone could read on the wire, or a Kerberos ticket. Better locks were promised for later.
